I found that the 350 odd nm holograms I made back in 87 or so were easily detectable using a spectrophotometer. If memory serves, I got an OD of about 1 (99% efficent) at about 350nm.

[quote:2a4ba595f4="JohnFP"]One way I think would be to make the hologram transmission, illuminated with UV source from the back and on the front put a dusting of florescent powder. It will flouresce at the layer of dusting with the wave front coming from the emulsion.

I also guess you would need the real image to be projected such that it comes in contact with the flourescent powder. Will this make the image look flat but with many views? I am not sure I can find a transmission hologram as I would like to see this effect.[/quote:2a4ba595f4]

I assume that the fluorescent material is butted right up against the plate and only on one side of it. In this case, you need to follow the wavefront as it starts off as a reconstruction wavefront and passes through the plate becoming an object wavefront on exit. This object wavefront is composed of phase factors that define it as a specific object wavefront and is basically the Fraunhofer pattern. However, when the wavefront hits the back of the hologram (the exit side) , it's a Fresnel diffraction pattern. If this Fresnel pattern causes fluorescent scattering within the fluorescent material, then a certain proportion will be fluorescently scattered and a certain proporrtion will not and will pass through the "scattering screen" and form the image. Thus, depending on the actual flourescent material and it's density, there will be a glow characterised by Fresnel diffraction and a loss in brightness of the image. If viewed, the hologram will appear to have a halo behind the image which may, or may not, be uniform depending on the exact object wavefront and the density of fluorescent matter. The proportion of "halo" to "image" will obviously depend on the density of fluorescent matter and the shape of the wavefront.

[quote:2a4ba595f4="JohnFP"]Is there a material that we can add to the emulsion such that the fringes bend the light, this light hits the flourescent material but still preserves the wave front thus enabling it to be viewed with a black light?[/quote:2a4ba595f4]

I never needed any special material. I did however need to alter the density according to Kramers Kronig. Basically, you need to look at the dispersion equation at the area of interest.

> I have been thinking about UV, how to peak the laser and see the beam, how to stear it etc..

I "peak" the UV laser I'm using the same way as a visible laser, with a power meter. I use a piece of fluorescent paper to find the beam (low power only or the paper burns). UV beamsplitters are difficult beasts and I'd recommend the high power one from Newport. UV microscope objectives are around $2000 each! Visible AR coatings are very reflective in the UV, and dielectric coated mirrors for the visible are not very reflective.

posts.author: Gary Deal
posts.content_md:
I take it that by shooting photos with a UV pass filter you mean on film? I was out of the game for a while and something may have changed, but photographing in UV may be a problem. As I understand it, gelatin is a pretty effective UV filter, which probably has a lot to do with why DCG works. Silver halide crystals embedded in the emulsion are pretty effectively masked from the UV, and specially sensitized UV films have to have the halides more or less sticking out of the front of the emulsion, which also makes it very delicate.

 However, the above information may be seventy years old. What do astronomers use to capture UV on film? Or do they bother?

 Using a broken black light bulb for a filter will probably just get you violet if it looks clear, or nothing if it's opaque (diffused) - like the inside of a fluorescent bulb. Don't typical fluorescent tubes produce a bunch of UV with the small amount of mercury vapor inside, which then excites the phosphor coating on the inside of the bulb, which then fluoresces brightly while it filters out all the UV? As an aside, I used to build machines that used long tube (quartz envelope) mercury vapor lamps, 100 watts per inch and 48 inches or more long. The power supplies were rather large. My repeated electrocutions are another story. 

How about taking the potential materials and applying them to a small flat surface. Have box of reasonable depth handy, laid on it's side, with a panel coated with a fluorescent material inside. In sunlight, using the flat test subject, attempt to refelect diffuse UV into the box at the fluorescent panel. If it glows in the shadows, the test material reflects UV. 

Please keep in mind that this is one of those "ideas" and I haven't tried it nor do I know if it will work. What could be used for a test material that's *known* to reflect UV at high percentages? You gotta have something that you know works so you have a standard to compare to.
